entities.summary:
The G-14, an exclusive consortium of elite European football clubs, emerged in 1998 and operated until its dissolution in 2008. Comprised initially of 14 prominent teams such as Manchester United, Real Madrid, and AC Milan, it aimed to enhance the commercial power and influence of its members within European football. This organization represented a critical shift in the governance of football, advocating for greater financial returns and autonomy from UEFA and FIFA, thereby reshaping the landscape of club football in Europe.

During its decade-long existence, the G-14 advocated for the interests of its member clubs, influencing negotiations related to broadcasting rights and the distribution of revenue from tournaments. By 2008, the group expanded to 18 clubs, reflecting its growing significance in European football. However, its tenure was marked by increasing tensions with UEFA and FIFA, culminating in a formal agreement that led to the establishment of the European Club Association, which now represents more than 240 clubs. This transition highlighted the ongoing struggle for power and profit within the realm of professional football.

The legacy of the G-14 is evident in its role in transforming the financial dynamics of European football, paving the way for more structured representation of clubs in negotiations with governing bodies. The establishment of the European Club Association can be seen as a direct consequence of the G-14's efforts, as it provided a more inclusive platform for clubs to voice their concerns and interests. This shift not only altered the financial landscape of football but also redefined the relationship between clubs and football authorities.
